text: May 1498. A Portuguese ship drops anchor off Calicut on India's southwest coast.
The captain sends one man ashore first, a convict in case things go wrong.
Do North African merchants spot him?
May the devil take you! What brought you here?
We came looking for Christians and spices.
That's in the ship's own journal.
All around him, sacks of black pepper and painted cotton cloth so fine that Europe would name
it after this very port, Calico.
Back then, India made about a quarter of everything the whole world produced.
That wealth pulled everyone in.
An emperor would apologize for a war in stone.
A diamond would travel from a peacock throne to the Tower of London and a trading company
would raise an army bigger than Britain's.
The numbers on your phone were first written here.
Even the English word loot is Hindi.
By 1950, India's share of the world was about 4%.
So how did the richest shop on earth get robbed again and again?
And why did almost every robber end up stank?
The answer starts in a city with better drains than many cities today and a writing system
nobody on earth can read.
In the 1850s, British engineers were building a railway across Punjab, from Lahore to Multan.
They had a problem.
A railway needs millions of bricks and Punjab had plenty of mud and very few stones.
When, near a village called Harappa, they found a hill made of bricks, old, hard, perfect
bricks, just lying in the ground.
Sir, there is an old ruin over there, full of bricks, free bricks, splendid, all ruins
never matter.
Sir, there are little stone stamps in here too, with animals on them.
Keep the stamps, ship the bricks.
